claims.claim: For speech in quiet at best intensity, the correlation between normal hearing and hearing loss dynamics after projection onto the first canonical component was 0.94 ± 0.01.
claims.source: When compared at best intensity (Figure 8a), there was good alignment between the dynamics for animals with normal hearing and hearing loss. The correlation for pairs of animals after projection onto the first CC, which accounted for 88 ± 2% and 71 ± 7% of the variance in animals with normal hearing (n = 6) and hearing loss (n = 6), respectively, was 0.94 ± 0.01 (n = 36).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the MCCA analysis for speech in quiet shown in Figure 8a.

claims.claim: For speech in quiet with a hearing aid, the correlation between normal hearing and hearing loss dynamics after projection onto the second canonical component was 0.73 ± 0.01.
claims.source: With the hearing aid (Figure 8b), the alignment between the dynamics for animals with normal hearing and hearing loss was even better. The correlation after projection onto the first CC remained high (0.94 ± 0.01; n = 36) and the correlation after projection onto the second CC rose substantially (0.73 ± 0.01; n = 36).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the MCCA analysis for speech in quiet with hearing aid shown in Figure 8b.

claims.claim: For speech in noise, the first canonical component accounted for 56 ± 1% of the variance for normal hearing animals but only 38 ± 7% for animals with hearing loss.
claims.source: But even for the first two CCs for which the alignment was relatively good, the percent of the variance accounted for by each was substantially different for normal hearing animals and those with hearing loss. The first CC, which provided a clean reflection of each consonant, accounted for 56 ± 1% of the variance for normal hearing animals (n = 6), but only 38 ± 7% of the variance for animals with hearing loss (n = 6).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the MCCA analysis for speech in noise shown in Figure 8c.

claims.claim: For speech in noise, the second canonical component accounted for 28 ± 1% of the variance for normal hearing animals but 41 ± 6% for animals with hearing loss.
claims.source: Conversely, the second CC, which was dominated by the background noise, accounted for 41 ± 6% of the variance for animals with hearing loss (n = 6), but only 28 ± 1% of the variance for animals with normal hearing.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the MCCA analysis for speech in noise shown in Figure 8c.

claims.claim: The balance of variance between neural subspaces encoding speech and background noise is tilted much more toward background noise in animals with hearing loss.
claims.source: Thus, while the neural subspaces encoding the speech and the background noise seem to be similar for all animals, the balance of variance between these subspaces is tilted much more toward background noise in animals with hearing loss.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the MCCA results for speech in noise.

claims.claim: Hearing loss allows the signal dynamics to be captured by background noise at the expense of foreground speech in a way that cannot be corrected by simple frequency-dependent amplification.
claims.source: Thus, it appears that hearing loss allows the signal dynamics to be captured by background noise at the expense of foreground speech in a way that cannot be corrected by simple frequency-dependent amplification.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the MCCA results for speech in noise with hearing aid.

claims.claim: For animals with normal hearing, the correlation between target only and target plus masker dynamics ranged from 0.25 to 0.75, with the masker having the largest impact when its center frequency was similar to that of the target.
claims.source: For animals with normal hearing, the correlation between the target only and target plus masker dynamics ranged from 0.25 to 0.75, with the masker having the largest impact when its center frequency was similar to that of the target (Figure 8f).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the narrowband target and masker analysis shown in Figure 8f.

claims.claim: When compared at the same high intensity, the correlation for animals with hearing loss was typically lower than normal when the masker center frequency was low, especially when the target center frequency was high.
claims.source: When compared at the same high intensity (70 dB SPL), the correlation for animals with hearing loss was typically lower than normal when the masker center frequency was low, especially when the target center frequency was high (Figure 8g).
claims.evidence: This is a qualitative observation from the narrowband target and masker analysis shown in Figure 8g.

claims.claim: Hearing loss creates deficits in spectral processing that manifest as highly nonlinear distortions in cross-frequency interactions that are particularly problematic for real-world speech in noise and cannot be corrected by simply compensating for lost sensitivity.
claims.source: Thus, hearing loss appears to create deficits in spectral processing that manifest as highly nonlinear distortions in cross-frequency interactions that are particularly problematic for real-world speech in noise and cannot be corrected by simply compensating for lost sensitivity.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the narrowband target and masker analysis results.

claims.claim: Changes in spectral processing, particularly in the interactions between different frequencies, are the primary problem caused by hearing loss.
claims.source: Our results suggest that changes in spectral processing, particularly in the interactions between different frequencies, are the primary problem.
claims.evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from all the experimental results.

claims.claim: Impaired spectral processing for simple tones does not appear to be a major problem for the neural coding of speech per se as suitable amplification corrected many of the distortions caused by hearing loss for speech in quiet.
claims.source: While impaired spectral processing was evident for simple tones as a clustering of dynamical trajectories within the signal manifold, this impairment does not appear to be a major problem for the neural coding of speech per se as suitable amplification corrected many of the distortions caused by hearing loss for speech in quiet.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the results for tones and speech in quiet.

claims.claim: The results are consistent with a recent study that found that hearing loss caused the IC activity patterns elicited by different phonemes to become less distinct, and that a hearing aid failed to correct this problem for speech in noise.
claims.source: These results are consistent with a recent study that found that hearing loss caused the IC activity patterns elicited by different phonemes to become less distinct, and that a hearing aid failed to correct this problem for speech in noise (Armstrong et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Armstrong et al., 2022.

claims.claim: Listeners with hearing loss struggle to combine temporal envelope cues across frequency channels.
claims.source: They are also consistent with a body of work demonstrating that listeners with hearing loss struggle to combine temporal envelope cues across frequency channels (Healy and Bacon, 2002; Healy and Carson, 2010; Souza and Boike, 2006; Grant et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: When speech is reduced to a single amplitude-modulated band, speech recognition performance is similar for all listeners, independent of their hearing status.
claims.source: When speech is reduced to a single amplitude-modulated band, speech recognition performance is similar for all listeners, independent of their hearing status, suggesting that temporal processing of the speech envelope per se is unaffected by hearing loss.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge from perceptual studies.

claims.claim: As additional amplitude-modulated bands are added to speech, performance increases more for normal hearing listeners than for those with hearing loss.
claims.source: But as additional amplitude-modulated bands are added, performance increases more for normal hearing listeners than for those with hearing loss, suggesting that the latter group are less able to make use of complementary temporal information across multiple frequency channels.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge from perceptual studies.

claims.claim: The difference in speech recognition performance is most pronounced when comparing the ability to make use of temporal modulations in high-frequency channels (4–6 kHz) in the presence of temporal modulations in lower frequency channels (1–2 kHz).
claims.source: This difference is most pronounced when comparing the ability to make use of temporal modulations in high-frequency channels (4–6 kHz) in the presence of temporal modulations in lower frequency channels (1–2 kHz) (Grant et al., 2007), and it does not appear to be a simple consequence of broadened frequency tuning but rather a specific deficit in cross-frequency interactions (Healy and Carson, 2010).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Grant et al., 2007 and Healy and Carson, 2010.

claims.claim: After hearing loss, the tuning curve 'tip' becomes less sensitive and may shift toward lower frequencies while the 'tail' may become more sensitive.
claims.source: After hearing loss, the tuning curve 'tip' (corresponding to the characteristic frequency [CF] to which the fiber is most sensitive) becomes less sensitive and may shift toward lower frequencies while the 'tail' (corresponding to frequencies below CF) may become more sensitive (Young, 2012).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Young, 2012.

claims.claim: In animals with mild-to-moderate sensorineural hearing loss, auditory nerve fibers with high CFs responded excessively to low-frequency sounds.
claims.source: One recent study has provided insight into how the complex spectral distortions in the cochlea impact the neural coding of speech in noise in the AN (Parida and Heinz, 2022). In animals with mild-to-moderate sensorineural hearing loss, fibers with high CFs responded excessively to low-frequency sounds and it was this effect (rather than changes in frequency selectivity per se or temporal processing) that appeared to be most responsible for the disrupted neural coding of speech in noise.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Parida and Heinz, 2022.

claims.claim: The distortion of spectral processing observed as clustering of network dynamics for simple tones in the IC does not appear to be present in the AN.
claims.source: The distortion of spectral processing that we observe as clustering of network dynamics for simple tones in the IC, however, does not appear to be present in the AN. It is difficult to be certain since no directly comparable analysis has been performed on experimental AN responses, but our analysis of simulated AN responses suggests that hearing loss has more complex effects on the signal dynamics in the AN than simply causing clustering (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from analysis of simulated AN responses shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Animals with hearing loss displayed behavioral hypersensitivity for detection of tones at the edge frequencies around which the hearing loss increased from mild to moderate.
claims.source: Distorted spectral processing has also recently been observed in the auditory cortex after mild-to-moderate sloping sensorineural hearing loss (McGill et al., 2022). Animals displayed behavioral hypersensitivity for detection of tones at the edge frequencies around which the hearing loss increased from mild to moderate as well as an overrepresentation of these frequencies in the cortical tonotopic map of BF.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to McGill et al., 2022.

claims.claim: Some cortical neurons tuned to edge frequencies exhibited increased neural gain and synchrony after hearing loss.
claims.source: Some cortical neurons tuned to these edge frequencies exhibited increased neural gain and synchrony, and direct stimulation of thalamocortical afferents demonstrated that hearing loss caused an increase in gain within the local cortical circuit.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on findings from McGill et al., 2022.

claims.claim: The complex suprathreshold effects of hearing loss present a difficult challenge for hearing aid designers.
claims.source: The complex suprathreshold effects of hearing loss that are evident in the distorted neural signal dynamics observed in this study present a difficult challenge for hearing aid designers.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings about the complexity of hearing loss effects.

claims.claim: Current hearing aids compensate for changes in the threshold and dynamic range of auditory processing using a framework built around a bank of bandpass filters with automatic gain control.
claims.source: Current hearing aids compensate for changes in the threshold and dynamic range of auditory processing using a framework built around a bank of bandpass filters with automatic gain control.
claims.evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about hearing aid design.

claims.claim: It is difficult to imagine how current hearing aid frameworks could be used to compensate for problems such as hypersensitivity to background noise that involve highly nonlinear interactions across frequency bands.
claims.source: The signal processing that can be performed by such a framework is highly constrained, and it is difficult to imagine how it could be used to compensate for problems such as hypersensitivity to background noise that involve highly nonlinear interactions across frequency bands.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of current hearing aid technology and the findings of the study.

claims.claim: Recent research on speech enhancement via DNNs has demonstrated the potential to yield dramatic improvements in performance.
claims.source: Recent research on speech enhancement via DNNs has demonstrated the potential to yield dramatic improvements in performance (Wang, 2017; Luo and Mesgarani, 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Wang, 2017 and Luo and Mesgarani, 2019.

claims.claim: Deep denoising may prove effective in situations with a single talker where it is obvious which sound is of interest.
claims.source: This 'deep denoising' may prove effective in situations with a single talker where it is obvious which sound is of interest.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the potential application of deep denoising.

claims.claim: There are many significant technical challenges that must be overcome before cognitive control of speech enhancement can be widely applied.
claims.source: It may be possible to implement cognitive control to direct enhancement toward the sound of interest but there are many significant technical challenges that must be overcome before this approach can be widely applied (Geirnaert et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Geirnaert et al., 2021.

claims.claim: It should be possible to identify optimal processing algorithms for hearing aids empirically by providing DNNs with the data they need to learn how best to transform sounds in order to elicit normal neural activity from an impaired auditory system.
claims.source: A more flexible alternative is to identify optimal processing algorithms for hearing aids empirically by providing DNNs with the data they need to learn how best to transform sounds in order to elicit normal neural activity from an impaired auditory system (Lesica, 2018; Drakopoulos and Verhulst, 2022).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lesica, 2018 and Drakopoulos and Verhulst, 2022.

claims.claim: The vast majority of people with hearing loss have only mild-to-moderate cochlear damage.
claims.source: But the vast majority of people with hearing loss have only mild-to-moderate cochlear damage (Wilson et al., 2017), and there should be sufficient functionality remaining within the auditory system for a hearing aid to leverage when attempting elicit the necessary patterns of neural activity.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wilson et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Current models of the cochlea can faithfully capture the transformation of incoming sound into basilar membrane motion and AN activity.
claims.source: Current models of the sensory periphery can be highly accurate. For example, there are numerous models of the cochlea that faithfully capture the transformation of incoming sound into basilar membrane motion and AN activity (Saremi et al., 2016; Verhulst et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Saremi et al., 2016 and Verhulst et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Models of sensory processing in the brain have generally been much less accurate than models of the sensory periphery.
claims.source: Models of sensory processing in the brain, however, have generally been much less accurate, with even the best models missing out on a significant fraction of the explainable variance in subcortical and cortical neural activity (Williamson et al., 2016; Rahman et al., 2020; McFarland et al., 2013; Vintch et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: A DNN trained to replicate an established model of the cochlea provided accurate and generalizable predictions of the model's response to speech and tones.
claims.source: Initial efforts to use DNNs to model the sensory periphery have shown that they can be as accurate as hand-designed biophysical models. In one recent study, a DNN trained to replicate an established model of the cochlea provided accurate and generalizable predictions of the model's response to speech and tones (Baby et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Baby et al., 2021.

claims.claim: A DNN trained on retinal ganglion cell activity predicted nearly all of the explainable variance in responses to natural images.
claims.source: In another study, a DNN trained on retinal ganglion cell activity predicted nearly all of the explainable variance in responses to natural images (Maheswaranathan et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Maheswaranathan et al., 2019.

claims.claim: DNN models of V1 responses to natural images explained 50 and 80% of the explainable variance in single-unit spike counts and calcium activity, respectively.
claims.source: DNN models of V1 responses to natural images explained 50 and 80% of the explainable variance in single-unit spike counts and calcium activity, respectively (Cadena et al., 2019; Walker et al., 2019), while DNN models of V4 explained 90% of the explainable variance in multi-unit spike counts (Bashivan et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cadena et al., 2019, Walker et al., 2019, and Bashivan et al., 2019.

claims.claim: DNN models of A1 responses to speech and other natural sounds explain much of the explainable variance in high-gamma activity, fMRI voxel responses, or time-varying spike rates.
claims.source: DNN models of A1 responses to speech and other natural sounds perform similarly well, explaining much of the explainable variance in high-gamma activity, fMRI voxel responses, or time-varying spike rates (Keshishian et al., 2020; Kell et al., 2018; Pennington and David, 2022).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Keshishian et al., 2020, Kell et al., 2018, and Pennington and David, 2022.

claims.claim: The DNN models in this study simulate neural activity with full temporal resolution, capturing spike times with millisecond precision.
claims.source: Our results improve on these initial successes in several important ways. Firstly, our models simulate neural activity with full temporal resolution, that is, spike times with millisecond precision.
claims.evidence: This describes a key feature of the DNN models developed in this study.

claims.claim: The activity produced by the DNN models is nearly indistinguishable from that recorded experimentally, capturing more than 95% of the explainable variance in many cases.
claims.source: Secondly, the activity produced by our models is nearly indistinguishable from that recorded experimentally, capturing more than 95% of the explainable variance in many cases.
claims.evidence: This describes the high accuracy of the DNN models developed in this study.

claims.claim: The use of a low-dimensional bottleneck in the DNN allows for high performance within a framework that also provides a compact and interpretable description of the latent dynamics.
claims.source: Finally, our use of a low-dimensional bottleneck allows us to achieve this performance within a framework that also provides a compact and interpretable description of the latent dynamics that underlie the full network activity patterns.
claims.evidence: This describes a key methodological advantage of the DNN approach used in this study.

claims.claim: It should now be possible to use computational models of the brain for exploratory basic research, with benefits that are both scientific and ethical.
claims.source: With these advances, it should now be possible to use computational models of the brain for exploratory basic research, with benefits that are both scientific (studies are no longer data limited) and ethical (animal experiments can be limited to confirmatory studies), as well as for technology development (such as improved hearing aids, as described above).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the potential applications of the DNN modeling approach.

claims.claim: With further effort, it may be possible to build models that not only simulate but also mirror the underlying structure of biological systems.
claims.source: With further effort, it may be possible to build models that are not only black-box simulators but also mirror the underlying structure of biological systems (Jazayeri and Ostojic, 2021; Chung and Abbott, 2021).

claims.source: All experimental protocols were approved by the UK Home Office (PPL P56840C21).
claims.evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the experiments.

results.result: Large-scale neural recordings were obtained from the inferior colliculus (IC) of gerbils using 512-channel electrode arrays, capturing multi-unit activity with millisecond temporal precision during presentation of speech and noise stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C28, C29, C119-C122 collectively describe the experimental methodology. The use of large-scale recordings (512 channels), the animal model (gerbils), temporal precision (1.3 ms bins), and ethical approval are all documented. The methodology is well-established and appropriately cited.

results.result: Signal correlations dominated over noise correlations in IC recordings, with signal variance accounting for 40% of overall variance but signal correlations accounting for 95% of total correlation between units.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C32 present quantitative measurements from the neural recordings shown in Figure 1c. The distinction between signal and noise is methodologically sound and consistent with prior work (Garcia-Lazaro et al., 2013). The measurements support the conclusion that signal correlations dominate.

results.result: The neural signal manifold for speech encoding in the IC is low-dimensional, requiring only 5-10 principal components to explain 95% of signal variance, and is highly consistent across normal hearing animals (96% variance explained).
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C33, C34 describe PCA results shown in Figures 2b-e. The low dimensionality is demonstrated through systematic analysis with appropriate train/test splits. The high cross-animal consistency (96%) validates that the signal manifold is fundamental and robust, not an artifact of individual recordings.

results.result: Hearing loss was induced via noise exposure, and the resulting signal manifold remained low-dimensional (4-7 PCs for 95% variance) with high consistency across hearing loss animals (95% variance explained).
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C37 describe the hearing loss induction protocol and PCA results for hearing loss animals shown in Figures 2f-h. The methodology follows established protocols (cited), and the results demonstrate that low-dimensional structure persists after hearing loss, though with altered dynamics.

results.result: Hearing loss profoundly distorts neural signal dynamics in a nonlinear manner, with only 78% similarity between normal hearing and hearing loss signal dynamics, indicating the distortion cannot be explained by linear transformation.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C38-C40 present the key finding that hearing loss fundamentally alters signal dynamics (Figure 2h-i). The 78% similarity is significantly lower than within-group comparisons (96% and 95%), and the inference that this represents nonlinear distortion is logically sound given that linear predictability would yield higher similarity.

results.result: Deep neural networks with bottleneck architectures accurately replicate IC neural activity, approaching 100% of explainable variance for high-quality units, with optimal performance at 8 bottleneck channels, while providing interpretable low-dimensional dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C41-C42, C114-C116 describe DNN performance shown in Figure 3c. The high accuracy (>95% explainable variance in many cases) and consistency with PCA dimensionality (8 channels) validate the approach. The bottleneck architecture successfully combines prediction accuracy with interpretability.

results.result: DNN-derived signal dynamics show 97% similarity within hearing status groups but only 87% similarity between normal hearing and hearing loss animals, consistent with PCA-based findings.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C44 present DNN-based cross-animal comparisons (Figure 3d-e). The results parallel the PCA findings (C34, C37, C38), providing independent validation. The slightly higher similarity (87% vs 78%) may reflect the DNN's ability to remove residual noise, as noted in the text.

results.result: DNNs trained on speech generalize to predict responses to pure tones (83% explainable variance) and, via transfer learning with frozen encoders, to new animals for SAM noise (85% explainable variance).
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C46 demonstrate DNN generalization (Figures 3f-g). The high performance on novel stimuli and new animals validates that the learned representations capture fundamental auditory processing. However, the authors appropriately note this is limited evidence and more extensive validation would strengthen the claim.

results.result: Hearing loss fundamentally disrupts spectral processing at the network level, causing trajectories for different tone frequencies to cluster into low and high frequency groups, with RDM similarity of only 0.59 at moderate intensity and 0.78 at best intensity, and CCA similarity of 0.37 and 0.88 respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C47-C52 describe spectral processing deficits shown in Figure 4. The clustering phenomenon is clearly visible in the dynamics (Figure 4d) and quantified through RSA and CCA. The persistence of distortion even at best intensity (0.78 RDM, 0.88 CCA vs. 0.91 and 0.98 for normal hearing) demonstrates suprathreshold effects beyond audibility.

results.result: Hearing loss has minimal impact on temporal processing beyond decreased audibility, with RDM similarity recovering from 0.76 at moderate intensity to 0.99 at best intensity, and CCA similarity recovering to 0.95.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C57 describe SAM noise results (Figure 5). The near-complete recovery of similarity at best intensity (0.99 RDM, 0.95 CCA) contrasts sharply with the persistent spectral deficits, supporting the conclusion that temporal processing is largely preserved. The inference (C57) is well-supported by the data.

results.result: For consonants in quiet, hearing loss reduces RDM similarity from 0.94 to 0.23 at conversational intensity, recovering to 0.87 at best intensity and 0.91 with hearing aid; decoding performance improves from 41% to 47% (best intensity) to 49% (hearing aid) compared to 55% for normal hearing, suggesting amplification largely corrects distortions.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C68 describe speech-in-quiet results (Figure 6). The progressive improvement with intensity and hearing aid amplification is well-documented. The inference (C68) that residual distortions are minor is supported by the near-normal RDM similarity (0.91) and modest decoding deficit (49% vs 55%), though statistical significance of the decoding difference should be verified.

results.result: For consonants in noise, hearing loss causes hypersensitivity to background noise that persists after amplification, with RDM similarity of only 0.15 at high intensity, improving to 0.62 (best intensity) or 0.56 (hearing aid) but remaining far below normal (0.89); decoding performance remains severely impaired at 22-23% compared to 32% for normal hearing.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C69-C77 describe speech-in-noise results (Figure 7). The persistent low similarity even with amplification (0.56-0.62 vs 0.89) and poor decoding (22-23% vs 32%) demonstrate that hearing aids fail to correct speech-in-noise deficits. Statistical comparisons (C73) confirm speech-in-noise is significantly worse than speech-in-quiet.

results.result: MCCA analysis reveals that for speech in noise, the balance of variance between neural subspaces encoding speech versus background noise is tilted toward noise in hearing loss animals (first CC: 56% vs 38% variance; second CC: 28% vs 41%), and this imbalance persists with hearing aid amplification.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C83 describe MCCA results (Figure 8a-d). The quantitative shift in variance allocation provides mechanistic insight into the hypersensitivity to background noise. The persistence with hearing aid (Figure 8d) explains why amplification fails to correct speech-in-noise deficits. The inference (C82-C83) is well-supported.

results.result: Hearing loss creates nonlinear distortions in cross-frequency interactions, with low-frequency maskers having increased disruptive effects on high-frequency targets (correlation typically lower than normal), and this distortion persists at best intensity and with hearing aid amplification.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C84-C86 describe narrowband target/masker results (Figure 8e-i). The increased disruption of high-frequency targets by low-frequency maskers directly demonstrates aberrant cross-frequency interactions. The persistence with amplification (Figure 8h-i) supports the conclusion that these are nonlinear distortions that cannot be corrected by simple gain adjustments.

results.result: Changes in spectral processing, particularly cross-frequency interactions, are the primary problem caused by hearing loss, though impaired spectral processing for simple tones does not appear to be a major problem for speech in quiet given that amplification corrects many distortions.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C88 synthesize findings across multiple experiments. The conclusion that spectral processing is the primary problem is supported by the contrast between preserved temporal processing (C57) and disrupted spectral processing (C52). The distinction between tones and speech-in-quiet (C88) is supported by comparing Figures 4 and 6.

results.result: Hearing loss is a widespread problem with significant societal impact, and while hearing aids are the only widely available treatment, they provide limited benefit in many settings, particularly for high-intensity sounds and speech in noise, due to poorly understood suprathreshold deficits.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C9-C17 establish the clinical and scientific context. These are well-established facts supported by appropriate citations (Wilson et al. 2017, WHO 2021, Lesica 2018, Moore 2007, Larson et al. 2000). The statement about clinical neglect (C17) is a reasonable inference from the lack of understanding (C16).

results.result: While consequences of cochlear damage are well-described at the auditory nerve level (decreased activity, lost synchrony capture, distorted tonotopy), few studies have compared neural coding in central areas before and after hearing loss, making it difficult to identify which peripheral changes are most important.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C24 review prior work on hearing loss effects. The citations (Young 2008, Miller et al. 1997, Henry et al. 2016, Armstrong et al. 2022) support the statements about auditory nerve changes and limited central studies. The characterization of the knowledge gap (C22) appropriately motivates the current study.

results.result: Neural coding in complex areas like the IC likely involves emergent network-level properties not apparent in individual neurons, and manifold learning techniques like PCA can identify compact representations that retain important features; gerbils are a common animal model for human hearing.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C27 establish the rationale for the methodological approach. The inference about emergent properties (C25) is reasonable given IC complexity. The description of manifold learning (C26) is supported by appropriate citations (Mitchell-Heggs et al. 2023, Williamson et al. 2019). The statement about gerbils (C27) is established knowledge.

results.result: The results are consistent with prior studies showing hearing loss impacts phoneme selectivity in IC, listeners struggle to combine temporal envelope cues across frequency channels, auditory nerve fibers with high CFs respond excessively to low-frequency sounds, and cortical neurons show altered gain and tonotopy.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C99 place results in context of prior work. All statements are supported by appropriate citations (Armstrong et al. 2022, Healy & Bacon 2002, Grant et al. 2007, Young 2012, Parida & Heinz 2022, McGill et al. 2022). The consistency with prior work strengthens confidence in the current findings.

results.result: The complex nonlinear effects of hearing loss present challenges for current hearing aid designs based on bandpass filters with automatic gain control; while DNN-based speech enhancement shows promise, and DNNs could potentially identify optimal processing algorithms empirically, significant technical challenges remain.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C106 discuss implications for hearing aid design. The characterization of current hearing aids (C101) is established knowledge. The inference about limitations (C102) follows logically from the nonlinear cross-frequency interactions demonstrated. Citations support statements about DNN speech enhancement (Wang 2017, Luo & Mesgarani 2019) and challenges (Geirnaert et al. 2021). The speculation about empirical optimization (C106) is appropriately tentative.

results.result: Most people with hearing loss have mild-to-moderate damage with sufficient remaining functionality for hearing aids to leverage; while peripheral models are highly accurate, brain models have been less accurate, but recent DNN approaches show promise for modeling sensory processing and could enable exploratory research and technology development.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C113, C117-C118 discuss the broader context of computational modeling. All factual statements are supported by appropriate citations (Wilson et al. 2017, Saremi et al. 2016, Verhulst et al. 2018, Baby et al. 2021, Maheswaranathan et al. 2019, Cadena et al. 2019, etc.). The speculations about future applications (C117-C118) are appropriately tentative.
